Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
never allow myself to feel or express anger

Threat.value: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
People are not what they seem

vignette: Arthur was sixty-eight when he finally sat in the intake room, his hands resting heavily on his knees. The trauma had unfolded years earlier, not with a gradual erosion of trust, but with a sudden, brutal ambush by a romantic partner in the narrow service lane behind his home. His abuser had pursued him on a bicycle, matching his frantic pace until Arthur felt the cold reality of being trapped between a moving frame and a brick wall. The violence that followed shattered his foundational beliefs about how the world works, leaving him convinced that people are not what they seem and that his own judgment was profoundly inadequate. When he later encountered a bicycle passing his office window, found himself alone with a female colleague in a cramped conference room, or navigated the packed aisles of a university hospital, those specific situations would instantly pull him back to the service lane. The environmental cues did not merely remind him of the past; they actively reinforced his catastrophic beliefs, convincing him that the world remained fundamentally hostile and that he was perpetually vulnerable. Over the ensuing months, his clinical environment became both a testing ground and a trap. Working as a psychologist in a bustling city practice, Arthur found that constant threat monitoring had rewired his nervous system. He woke during the night repeatedly, convinced a break-in was imminent, and found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day because the darkness amplifies every shadow. Because he believed the world was shattered and people were untrustworthy, this night-time uncertainty cemented his negative appraisals, while his hypervigilance, in turn, made him interpret neutral stimuli like bicycles and crowded rooms as immediate threats. His conviction that he was inadequate and that others were dangerous actively heightened his sensitivity to these triggers, so a passing bicycle or a sudden crowd instantly registered as danger. To survive the daytime, he enacted strict behavioral controls. He began avoiding wearing similar clothes to his abuser, not out of aesthetic preference, but because the fabric against his skin felt like a trigger waiting to ignite panic. When crowds pressed around him at departmental seminars or when he had to be alone with a woman to discuss a case, his body would stiffen, his eyes would dart across the room looking for harm, and he would never allow himself to feel or express anger. He told himself he was maintaining professional decorum, but the rigid suppression of his emotions only served to isolate the trauma further. His constant checking and night-time alertness prevented proper memory processing, leaving recall stuck in disjointed, photographic frames of that afternoon, or flooded him with raw fear completely divorced from any clear image. By refusing to process the emotional intensity of the event, he ensured his recall remained fragmented. The inability to tell a coherent story of the event only deepened his sense of inadequacy, proving to him that he could not even process the trauma correctly. These fragmented recollections, in turn, solidified his conviction that people are not what they seem, turning every professional interaction into a potential threat. The avoidance of certain garments and the emotion control only heightened his sensitivity to environmental cues, so a sudden bicycle bell or a shift in a crowded hallway would immediately spike his heart rate and pull him back into that initial paralysis. Now, after years of functioning on autopilot while his marriage frayed under the weight of his distance, Arthur had come to believe that his own coping mechanisms were failing him. He sought help not because he wanted to relive the abuse, but because the tighter the cycle grew, the less he could trust his own perception of reality. He hoped to regain a sense of safety that no longer depended on constant vigilance, afraid that another year of suppression would leave him completely isolated from the life and relationships he still valued.
